title: GraphP-FL: Personalized Federated Graph Learning with Noisy Networks
one_liner: When several sites train a graph model together without sharing raw data, fix broken network links and track which parameters matter most to stop forgetting.
lead: Federated graph learning means separate organizations train a neural model together on graph-shaped data—social networks, chemical molecules—without sending raw data to a center. The problem: local graphs are often incomplete or wrong (missing links, bad connections), and when models average their numbers (the weights that control predictions) globally, they forget what worked locally. This paper fixes both: it rebuilds broken graph links using patterns found in the data itself, and protects the numbers that matter most during averaging so local knowledge survives.

problem.h2: Two blockers in federated graph learning
paras: When a graph neural network trains across multiple sites—a hospital network, social-media companies, research labs—no one sends raw data to a center, keeping privacy intact. Each site learns on its own graph structure. But graphs in the real world are messy: links are missing, connections point to the wrong nodes. A naive approach trains on these broken graphs as-is and averages all weights equally during synchronization, treating a weight that memorized a patient list exactly like one that caught a broad pattern.

This breaks in two ways. First, topological noise (wrong or missing edges) corrupts the representations each site learns—the model memorizes bad structure. Second, when you average model weights globally, you erase the critical local knowledge that site's graph taught. This is catastrophic forgetting: the combined model becomes weaker on each site's private task.

callout.html: Before each averaging step, repair noisy graph links using data patterns, and slow the movement of each number (weight) based on its importance so the critical ones resist averaging.

paras: First, the paper changes which edges exist in the local graph—it removes noise and adds missing links using self-supervised learning, a method that learns from unlabeled data by predicting masked-out parts of the input. Second, it changes how much each parameter moves during global averaging: important parameters resist change, others drift toward the global mean.

hidden.name: Fisher information per weight
paras: Every model weight (the numbers controlling the predictions) contributes differently to learning. A weight that only affects predictions on rare patient types matters less than one affecting common patterns. The paper measures this with Fisher information: a score calculated from how much the gradient (the direction to adjust the weight for lower error) wiggles around. Large wiggles mean the weight is sensitive to the data—change it, the loss changes a lot. Small wiggles mean it is dormant on this site's data.

The paper calculates Fisher scores on each site's private data, then uses those scores during global averaging. High-importance weights barely move toward the global average. Low-importance ones move freely. This preserves each site's local discoveries while allowing beneficial global patterns to spread.

heat.caption: Darker weights have higher Fisher importance on this site's data.

reads.html: Some weights control accurate predictions on this site's data; others are dormant. You want to measure which is which before averaging, then protect the ones controlling accuracy.

Fisher information measures how sensitive the predictions are to each weight—if the gradient (direction to adjust the weight) wiggles a lot on this site's data, the weight must matter for these predictions, so it gets a high importance score. The paper uses diagonal Fisher (a simplified version that looks at one weight at a time instead of all interactions together) to compute these scores and weight the elastic penalty term during averaging.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: two mechanisms in parallel
paras: Mechanism 1: Fixing the graph. Real-world graphs have missing edges and noise. The paper repairs them using self-supervised learning: it masks out a portion of edges and trains the graph model to predict which ones should exist based on node features and the remaining structure. This forces the model to learn hidden dependencies—if node A and B share similar neighbors and features, the model infers they should be linked. After training, the model predicts missing edges and corrects false ones. Now the local graph is cleaner: instead of learning on broken structure, the model processes true relationships, so it encodes what matters into each node's learned representation without contamination from phantom or absent edges.

Mechanism 2: Elastic parameter alignment. After all sites train and send weights to the center, the center averages them (standard federated learning). But this averaging erases each site's hard-won local knowledge. The paper then pulls each weight back toward its local value by an amount proportional to its Fisher importance score. A weight with Fisher score 10 pulls back twice as hard as one with score 5. Critical weights (those that shaped local representations) barely move. Unimportant ones move nearly all the way to the global average. The result: local knowledge survives, but beneficial global patterns still propagate across sites.

items.b: Graph repair fails on highly incomplete graphs.
items.html: If a site's graph is missing most edges, self-supervised learning has too little signal to infer the missing structure. The repair adds noise instead of signal. For extremely sparse or adversarial graphs, the method may not recover enough.

items.b: Fisher scores computed on small or biased local data are unreliable.
items.html: If a site has only 50 samples of patient data, the Fisher scores may be noisy—the importance ranking fluctuates. An unimportant weight looks important by chance, so it resists averaging too much, blocking global learning.

If lambda (the strength of elastic pull) is too high, weights stay too local and sites ignore global patterns. If too low, the method collapses to naive averaging. Finding the right lambda requires tuning per dataset.

items.b: Done right: diverse heterogeneous graphs and small Fisher estimates.
items.html: The method works best when sites have genuinely different graph structures (each repairs its own structure independently) and sufficient local data to compute reliable Fisher scores. The elastic alignment then preserves what is truly local while enabling beneficial global averaging.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a federated graph learning setup on two or three simple datasets (e.g., a social-network graph split across sites with intentional edge noise added, or a molecular-property dataset split by molecule type). Corrupt each local graph by removing or flipping 20% of edges. Train the graph model (a graph neural network) on each site for several rounds. Measure accuracy on held-out test data at each site before and after receiving global-averaged weights. Repeat three times: once with naive averaging, once with elastic alignment using constant Fisher estimates (all equal), and once with elastic alignment using true Fisher scores. The demo succeeds when elastic alignment preserves >80% of local accuracy while naive averaging drops accuracy by 30+ percentage points.
demo.metric_eq: forgetting = accuracy_before_averaging - accuracy_after_averaging. Catastrophic forgetting shows as forgetting > 25%. Elastic alignment shows forgetting < 10%.
demo.closing: The demo must show that protecting important parameters measurably stops the local accuracy collapse that happens with naive averaging.
